title: Power And Corruption (Lord Acton’s Observation In Action)
description: Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely. More precisely, power reduces empathy, increases self‑focus, and makes people more likely to act on their impulses, including selfish or unethical ones.
shortDescription: Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely. More precisely, power reduces empathy, increases self‑focus, and makes people more likely to act on their impulses, including selfish or unethical ones.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely. More precisely, power reduces empathy, increases self‑focus, and makes people more likely to act on their impulses, including selfish or unethical ones.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A new manager who was once a supportive peer starts interrupting, ignoring input, and taking credit.
A politician who campaigned on integrity becomes entangled in scandals after years in office.
A wealthy individual starts treating service workers as invisible or beneath them.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Reduced eye contact with “lower‑status” people; seeing them as a means to an end.
Increased risk‑taking because they feel invulnerable.
Speaking over others and showing impatience with alternative views.
Moral disengagement: using euphemisms to justify harmful actions (“It’s just business”).

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “I don’t have time for this.” (to someone who needs help)
“You don’t understand the pressure I’m under.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You notice you’re treating people differently based on what they can do for you.
You feel irritated when someone questions your decision.
You’ve started to believe that your success is entirely your own doing and that others are simply less capable.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Studies by Dacher Keltner and others show that power activates the brain’s reward system and reduces the activity of mirror neurons, dampening empathy. It also makes people more likely to act on their desires without inhibition (the “approach” theory of power).

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: If you gain power, deliberately build in accountability: a trusted advisor who will tell you hard truths, regular exposure to those affected by your decisions, and habits of gratitude.
Notice when you start to dehumanize or dismiss others. That’s the early warning signal.
Rotate power or limit terms; institutionalize checks so that power doesn’t concentrate and corrode.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Believing it won’t happen to you because you’re a “good person.” The effect is situational, not character‑based.
Using the phrase “I’ve earned the right to…” as a justification for special treatment.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A CEO who started the company with a mission to “treat people well” now has a private jet, a personal chef, and an executive floor that no regular employee can access. He hasn’t spoken to a front‑line worker in a year. His decisions become disconnected from reality, and the company culture rots. He’s not evil; he’s isolated by his own power bubble.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: Power is a mirror. It doesn’t change you; it reveals what was always inside, and then magnifies it until it’s all you can see.
